Although Diem was publicly praised, in private Secretary of State John Foster Dulles conceded that Diem had been selected because there were no better alternatives.<sup id="cite_ref-236" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-236">&#91;236&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After the election of November 1960, Eisenhower, in a briefing with <a href="/wiki/John_F._Kennedy" title="John F. Kennedy">John F. Kennedy</a>, pointed out the communist threat in Southeast Asia as requiring prioritization in the next administration. Eisenhower told Kennedy he considered Laos "the cork in the bottle" with regard to the regional threat.<sup id="cite_ref-237" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-237">&#91;237&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Legitimation_of_Francoist_Spain">Legitimation of Francoist Spain</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Pact_of_Madrid" title="Pact of Madrid">Pact of Madrid</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Franco_eisenhower_1959_madrid.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Franco_eisenhower_1959_madrid.jpg/220px-Franco_eisenhower_1959_madrid.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="155" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Franco_eisenhower_1959_madrid.jpg/330px-Franco_eisenhower_1959_madrid.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Franco_eisenhower_1959_madrid.jpg/440px-Franco_eisenhower_1959_madrid.jpg 2x" data-file-width="607" data-file-height="428" /></a><figcaption>Spanish dictator <a href="/wiki/Francisco_Franco" title="Francisco Franco">Francisco Franco</a> and Eisenhower in <a href="/wiki/Madrid" title="Madrid">Madrid</a> in 1959.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Pact of Madrid, signed on September 23, 1953, by <a href="/wiki/Francoist_Spain" title="Francoist Spain">Francoist Spain</a> and the United States, was a significant effort to break <a href="/wiki/International_isolation" title="International isolation">international isolation</a> of Spain after <a href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</a>, together with the <a href="/wiki/Concordat_of_1953" title="Concordat of 1953">Concordat of 1953</a>. This development came at a time when other victorious <a href="/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II" title="Allies of World War II">Allies of World War II</a> and much of the rest of the world remained hostile (for the 1946 United Nations condemnation<sup id="cite_ref-238" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-238">&#91;238&#93;</a></sup> of the Francoist regime, see "<a href="/wiki/Spanish_Question_(United_Nations)" class="mw-redirect" title="Spanish Question (United Nations)">Spanish Question</a>") to a <a href="/wiki/Fascism" title="Fascism">fascist</a> regime sympathetic to the cause of the former <a href="/wiki/Axis_powers" title="Axis powers">Axis powers</a> and <a href="/wiki/German_involvement_in_the_Spanish_Civil_War" title="German involvement in the Spanish Civil War">established with Nazi assistance</a>. This accord took the form of three separate executive agreements that pledged the United States to furnish <a href="/wiki/Foreign_aid" class="mw-redirect" title="Foreign aid">economic</a> and <a href="/wiki/Military_aid" title="Military aid">military aid</a> to Spain. 
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="The_Middle_East_and_Eisenhower_doctrine">The Middle East and Eisenhower doctrine</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:ShahEisenhower.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/ShahEisenhower.jpg/170px-ShahEisenhower.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="209" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/ShahEisenhower.jpg/255px-ShahEisenhower.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/ShahEisenhower.jpg/340px-ShahEisenhower.jpg 2x" data-file-width="400" data-file-height="491" /></a><figcaption>Eisenhower with the Shah of Iran, <a href="/wiki/Mohammad_Reza_Pahlavi" title="Mohammad Reza Pahlavi">Mohammad Reza Pahlavi</a> (1959)</figcaption></figure>
<p>Even before he was inaugurated Eisenhower accepted a request from the British government to restore the Shah of Iran (<a href="/wiki/Mohammad_Reza_Pahlavi" title="Mohammad Reza Pahlavi">Mohammad Reza Pahlavi</a>) to power. He therefore <a href="/wiki/1953_Iranian_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat" title="1953 Iranian coup d&#39;état">authorized the Central Intelligence Agency</a> to overthrow Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Mohammad_Mosaddegh" title="Mohammad Mosaddegh">Mohammad Mosaddegh</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-239" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-239">&#91;239&#93;</a></sup> This resulted in increased strategic control over Iranian oil by <a href="/wiki/Seven_Sisters_(oil_companies)" class="mw-redirect" title="Seven Sisters (oil companies)">U.S. and British companies</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-240" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-240">&#91;240&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In November 1956, Eisenhower forced an end to the combined British, French and Israeli invasion of Egypt in response to the <a href="/wiki/Suez_Crisis" title="Suez Crisis">Suez Crisis</a>, receiving praise from Egyptian president <a href="/wiki/Gamal_Abdel_Nasser" title="Gamal Abdel Nasser">Gamal Abdel Nasser</a>. Simultaneously he condemned the brutal Soviet invasion of <a href="/wiki/Hungarian_People%27s_Republic" title="Hungarian People&#39;s Republic">Hungary</a> in response to the <a href="/wiki/Hungarian_Revolution_of_1956" title="Hungarian Revolution of 1956">Hungarian Revolution of 1956</a>. He publicly disavowed his allies at the United Nations and used financial and diplomatic pressure to make them withdraw from Egypt.<sup id="cite_ref-241" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-241">&#91;241&#93;</a></sup> Eisenhower explicitly defended his strong position against Britain and France in his memoirs, which were published in 1965.<sup id="cite_ref-242" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-242">&#91;242&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After the Suez Crisis, the United States became the protector of unstable friendly governments in the Middle East via the "<a href="/wiki/Eisenhower_Doctrine" title="Eisenhower Doctrine">Eisenhower Doctrine</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-243" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-243">&#91;243&#93;</a></sup> Designed by Secretary of State Dulles, it held the U.S. would be "prepared to use armed force&#160;... [to counter] aggression from any country controlled by international communism". Further, the United States would provide economic and military aid and, if necessary, use military force to stop the spread of communism in the Middle East.<sup id="cite_ref-244" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-244">&#91;244&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Eisenhower_and_Nixon_at_Dinner_with_King_Saud.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Eisenhower_and_Nixon_at_Dinner_with_King_Saud.jpg/220px-Eisenhower_and_Nixon_at_Dinner_with_King_Saud.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="166" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Eisenhower_and_Nixon_at_Dinner_with_King_Saud.jpg/330px-Eisenhower_and_Nixon_at_Dinner_with_King_Saud.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Eisenhower_and_Nixon_at_Dinner_with_King_Saud.jpg/440px-Eisenhower_and_Nixon_at_Dinner_with_King_Saud.jpg 2x" data-file-width="635" data-file-height="480" /></a><figcaption>Eisenhower and Vice President <a href="/wiki/Richard_Nixon" title="Richard Nixon">Richard Nixon</a> with their host, King <a href="/wiki/Saud_of_Saudi_Arabia" title="Saud of Saudi Arabia">Saud of Saudi Arabia</a>, at the <a href="/wiki/Mayflower_Hotel" title="Mayflower Hotel">Mayflower Hotel</a> (1957)</figcaption></figure>
<p>Eisenhower applied the doctrine in 1957–1958 by dispensing economic aid to shore up the Kingdom of Jordan, and by encouraging Syria's neighbors to consider military operations against it. More dramatically, in July 1958, he sent 15,000 <a href="/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps" title="United States Marine Corps">Marines</a> and soldiers to Lebanon as part of <a href="/wiki/Operation_Blue_Bat" class="mw-redirect" title="Operation Blue Bat">Operation Blue Bat</a>, a non-combat peace-keeping mission to stabilize the pro-Western government and to prevent a radical revolution from sweeping over that country.<sup id="cite_ref-Little_1996_27–54_245-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Little_1996_27–54-245">&#91;245&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The mission proved a success and the Marines departed three months later. The deployment came in response to the urgent request of Lebanese president <a href="/wiki/Camille_Chamoun" title="Camille Chamoun">Camille Chamoun</a> after sectarian violence had erupted in the country. Washington considered the military intervention successful since it brought about regional stability, weakened Soviet influence, and intimidated the Egyptian and Syrian governments, whose anti-West political position had hardened after the Suez Crisis.<sup id="cite_ref-Little_1996_27–54_245-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Little_1996_27–54-245">&#91;245&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Most Arab countries were skeptical about the "Eisenhower doctrine" because they considered "Zionist imperialism" the real danger. However, they did take the opportunity to obtain free money and weapons. Egypt and Syria, supported by the Soviet Union, openly opposed the initiative. However, Egypt received American aid until the <a href="/wiki/Six-Day_War" title="Six-Day War">Six-Day War</a> in 1967.<sup id="cite_ref-246" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-246">&#91;246&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As the <a href="/wiki/Cold_War" title="Cold War">Cold War</a> deepened, Dulles sought to isolate the <a href="/wiki/Soviet_Union" title="Soviet Union">Soviet Union</a> by building regional alliances of nations against it. Critics sometimes called it "<a href="/wiki/Pactomania" title="Pactomania">pacto-mania</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-247" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-247">&#91;247&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="1960_U-2_incident">1960 U-2 incident</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/1960_U-2_incident" title="1960 U-2 incident">1960 U-2 incident</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:US_Air_Force_U-2_(2139646280).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/US_Air_Force_U-2_%282139646280%29.jpg/220px-US_Air_Force_U-2_%282139646280%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="176" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/US_Air_Force_U-2_%282139646280%29.jpg/330px-US_Air_Force_U-2_%282139646280%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/US_Air_Force_U-2_%282139646280%29.jpg/440px-US_Air_Force_U-2_%282139646280%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="2400" /></a><figcaption>A <a href="/wiki/Lockheed_U-2" title="Lockheed U-2">U-2</a> reconnaissance aircraft in flight</figcaption></figure>
<p>On May 1, 1960, a U.S. one-man <a href="/wiki/Lockheed_U-2" title="Lockheed U-2">U-2</a> spy plane was shot down at high altitude over Soviet airspace. The flight was made to gain photo intelligence before the scheduled opening of an east–west summit conference, which had been scheduled in Paris, 15 days later.<sup id="cite_ref-248" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-248">&#91;248&#93;</a></sup> Captain <a href="/wiki/Francis_Gary_Powers" title="Francis Gary Powers">Francis Gary Powers</a> had bailed out of his aircraft and was captured after parachuting down onto Russian soil. Four days after Powers disappeared, the Eisenhower Administration had NASA issue a very detailed press release noting that an aircraft had "gone missing" north of Turkey. It speculated that the pilot might have fallen unconscious while the <a href="/wiki/Autopilot" title="Autopilot">autopilot</a> was still engaged, and falsely claimed that "the pilot reported over the emergency frequency that he was experiencing oxygen difficulties."<sup id="cite_ref-Russian_officer_249-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Russian_officer-249">&#91;249&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Soviet Premier <a href="/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev" title="Nikita Khrushchev">Nikita Khrushchev</a> announced that a "spy-plane" had been shot down but intentionally made no reference to the pilot. As a result, the Eisenhower Administration, thinking the pilot had died in the crash, authorized the release of a cover story claiming that the plane was a "weather research aircraft" which had unintentionally strayed into Soviet airspace after the pilot had radioed "difficulties with his oxygen equipment" while flying over Turkey.<sup id="cite_ref-250" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-250">&#91;250&#93;</a></sup> The Soviets put Captain Powers on trial and displayed parts of the U-2, which had been recovered almost fully intact.<sup id="cite_ref-The_Cold_War_251-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-The_Cold_War-251">&#91;251&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Four Power Paris Summit in May 1960 with Eisenhower, Nikita Khrushchev, <a href="/wiki/Harold_Macmillan" title="Harold Macmillan">Harold Macmillan</a> and <a href="/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle" title="Charles de Gaulle">Charles de Gaulle</a> collapsed because of the incident. Eisenhower refused to accede to Khrushchev's demands that he apologize. Therefore, Khrushchev would not take part in the summit. Up until this event, Eisenhower felt he had been making progress towards better relations with the Soviet Union. Nuclear arms reduction and Berlin were to have been discussed at the summit. Eisenhower stated it had all been ruined because of that "stupid U-2 business".<sup id="cite_ref-The_Cold_War_251-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-The_Cold_War-251">&#91;251&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The affair was an embarrassment for United States prestige. Further, the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Foreign_Relations" title="United States Senate Committee on Foreign Relations">Senate Foreign Relations Committee</a> held a lengthy inquiry into the U-2 incident.<sup id="cite_ref-The_Cold_War_251-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-The_Cold_War-251">&#91;251&#93;</a></sup> In Russia, Captain Powers made a forced confession and apology. On August 19, 1960, Powers was convicted of espionage and sentenced to imprisonment. On February 10, 1962, Powers was exchanged for <a href="/wiki/Rudolf_Abel" title="Rudolf Abel">Rudolf Abel</a> in Berlin and returned to the U.S.<sup id="cite_ref-Russian_officer_249-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Russian_officer-249">&#91;249&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Civil_rights">Civil rights</span></h3>
<p>While President Truman's 1948 <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_9981" title="Executive Order 9981">Executive Order 9981</a> had begun the process of <a href="/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States_Armed_Forces" title="Racial segregation in the United States Armed Forces">desegregating the Armed Forces</a>, actual implementation had been slow. Eisenhower made clear his stance in his first <a href="/wiki/State_of_the_Union_address" class="mw-redirect" title="State of the Union address">State of the Union address</a> in February 1953, saying "I propose to use whatever authority exists in the office of the President to end segregation in the District of Columbia, including the <a href="/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States" title="Federal government of the United States">Federal Government</a>, and any segregation in the Armed Forces".<sup id="cite_ref-252" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-252">&#91;252&#93;</a></sup> When he encountered opposition from the services, he used government control of military spending to force the change through, stating "Wherever Federal Funds are expended&#160;..., I do not see how any American can justify&#160;... a discrimination in the expenditure of those funds".<sup id="cite_ref-253" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-253">&#91;253&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>When <a href="/wiki/Robert_B._Anderson" title="Robert B. Anderson">Robert B. Anderson</a>, Eisenhower's first <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_the_Navy" class="mw-redirect" title="Secretary of the Navy">Secretary of the Navy</a>, argued that the <a href="/wiki/U.S._Navy" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Navy">U.S. Navy</a> must recognize the "customs and usages prevailing in certain geographic areas of our country which the Navy had no part in creating," Eisenhower overruled him: "We have not taken and we shall not take a single backward step. There must be no second class citizens in this country."<sup id="cite_ref-254" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-254">&#91;254&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The administration declared <a href="/wiki/Racial_discrimination" title="Racial discrimination">racial discrimination</a> a <a href="/wiki/National_security" title="National security">national security</a> issue, as Communists around the world used the racial discrimination and history of violence in the U.S. as a point of propaganda attack.<sup id="cite_ref-255" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-255">&#91;255&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Eisenhower told <a href="/wiki/Washington,_D.C." title="Washington, D.C.">Washington, D.C.</a> officials to make the city a model for the rest of the country in integrating black and white public-school children.<sup id="cite_ref-256" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-256">&#91;256&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-257" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-257">&#91;257&#93;</a></sup> He proposed to Congress the <a href="/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1957" title="Civil Rights Act of 1957">Civil Rights Act of 1957</a> and <a href="/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1960" title="Civil Rights Act of 1960">of 1960</a> and signed those acts into law. The 1957 act for the first time established a permanent civil rights office inside the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice" title="United States Department of Justice">Justice Department</a> and a <a href="/wiki/Civil_Rights_Commission" class="mw-redirect" title="Civil Rights Commission">Civil Rights Commission</a> to hear testimony about abuses of voting rights. Although both acts were much weaker than subsequent civil rights legislation, they constituted the first significant civil rights acts <a href="/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1875" title="Civil Rights Act of 1875">since 1875</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-258" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-258">&#91;258&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1957 the state of <a href="/wiki/Arkansas" title="Arkansas">Arkansas</a> refused to honor a federal court order to integrate their public school system stemming from the <i><a href="/wiki/Brown_v._Board_of_Education" title="Brown v. Board of Education">Brown</a></i> decision. Eisenhower demanded that Arkansas governor <a href="/wiki/Orval_Faubus" title="Orval Faubus">Orval Faubus</a> obey the court order. When Faubus balked, the president placed the <a href="/wiki/Arkansas_Army_National_Guard" title="Arkansas Army National Guard">Arkansas National Guard</a> under federal control and sent in the <a href="/wiki/101st_Airborne_Division" title="101st Airborne Division">101st Airborne Division</a>. They escorted and protected <a href="/wiki/Little_Rock_Nine" title="Little Rock Nine">nine black students</a>' entry to <a href="/wiki/Little_Rock_Central_High_School" title="Little Rock Central High School">Little Rock Central High School</a>, an all-white public school, marking the first time since the <a href="/wiki/Reconstruction_Era" class="mw-redirect" title="Reconstruction Era">Reconstruction Era</a> the federal government had used federal troops in the South to enforce the U. S. Constitution.<sup id="cite_ref-259" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-259">&#91;259&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr." title="Martin Luther King Jr.">Martin Luther King Jr.</a> wrote to Eisenhower to thank him for his actions, writing "The overwhelming majority of southerners, Negro and white, stand firmly behind your resolute action to restore law and order in <a href="/wiki/Little_Rock,_Arkansas" title="Little Rock, Arkansas">Little Rock</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-260" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-260">&#91;260&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Eisenhower's administration contributed to the McCarthyist <a href="/wiki/Lavender_Scare" title="Lavender Scare">Lavender Scare</a><sup id="cite_ref-261" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-261">&#91;261&#93;</a></sup> with President Eisenhower issuing <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_10450" title="Executive Order 10450">Executive Order 10450</a> in 1953.<sup id="cite_ref-262" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-262">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup> During Eisenhower's presidency thousands of <a href="/wiki/LGBT" title="LGBT">lesbian and gay</a> applicants were barred from federal employment and over 5,000 federal employees were fired under suspicions of being homosexual.<sup id="cite_ref-documenting_263-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-documenting-263">&#91;263&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-264" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-264">&#91;264&#93;</a></sup> From 1947 to 1961 the number of firings based on sexual orientation were far greater than those for membership in the <a href="/wiki/Communist_Party_USA" title="Communist Party USA">Communist Party</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-documenting_263-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-documenting-263">&#91;263&#93;</a></sup> and government officials intentionally campaigned to make "homosexual" synonymous with "Communist traitor" such that LGBT people were treated as a national security threat stemming from the belief they were susceptible to blackmail and exploitation.<sup id="cite_ref-265" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-265">&#91;265&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Relations_with_Congress">Relations with Congress</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Dwight_D._Eisenhower,_official_Presidential_portrait.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Dwight_D._Eisenhower%2C_official_Presidential_portrait.jpg/220px-Dwight_D._Eisenhower%2C_official_Presidential_portrait.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="281" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Dwight_D._Eisenhower%2C_official_Presidential_portrait.jpg/330px-Dwight_D._Eisenhower%2C_official_Presidential_portrait.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Dwight_D._Eisenhower%2C_official_Presidential_portrait.jpg/440px-Dwight_D._Eisenhower%2C_official_Presidential_portrait.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2345" data-file-height="3000" /></a><figcaption>Official White House Portrait of President Eisenhower, <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;">&#8201;1960</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>Eisenhower had a Republican Congress for only his first two years in office; in the Senate, Republicans held the majority by a one-vote margin. Despite being Eisenhower's political opponent for the 1952 Republican presidential nomination, Senator Majority Leader <a href="/wiki/Robert_A._Taft" title="Robert A. Taft">Robert A. Taft</a> assisted Eisenhower a great deal by promoting the President's proposals among the "Old Guard" Republican Senators. Taft's death in July 1953 - six months into Eisenhower's presidency - affected Eisenhower both personally and professionally. The President noted he had lost "a dear friend" with Taft's passing. Eisenhower disliked Taft's successor as Majority Leader, Senator <a href="/wiki/William_Knowland" title="William Knowland">William Knowland</a>, and the relationship between the two men led to tension between the Senate and the White House.<sup id="cite_ref-266" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-266">&#91;266&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>This prevented Eisenhower from openly condemning Joseph McCarthy's highly criticized methods against communism. To facilitate relations with Congress, Eisenhower decided to ignore McCarthy's controversies and thereby deprive them of more energy from the involvement of the White House. This position drew criticism from a number of corners.<sup id="cite_ref-267" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-267">&#91;267&#93;</a></sup> In late 1953, McCarthy declared on national television that the employment of communists within the government was a menace and would be a pivotal issue in the <a href="/wiki/1954_United_States_Senate_elections" title="1954 United States Senate elections">1954 Senate elections</a>. Eisenhower was urged to respond directly and specify the various measures he had taken to purge the government of communists.<sup id="cite_ref-268" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-268">&#91;268&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Among Eisenhower's objectives in not directly confronting McCarthy was to prevent McCarthy from dragging the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Atomic_Energy_Commission" title="United States Atomic Energy Commission">Atomic Energy Commission</a> (AEC) into McCarthy's witch hunt for communists, which might interfere with the AEC's work on <a href="/wiki/Hydrogen_bomb" class="mw-redirect" title="Hydrogen bomb">hydrogen bombs</a> and other weapons programs.<sup id="cite_ref-269" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-269">&#91;269&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-y-s-132_270-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-y-s-132-270">&#91;270&#93;</a></sup> In December 1953, Eisenhower learned that one of America's nuclear scientists, <a href="/wiki/J._Robert_Oppenheimer" title="J. Robert Oppenheimer">J. Robert Oppenheimer</a>, had been accused of being a spy for the <a href="/wiki/Soviet_Union" title="Soviet Union">Soviet Union</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-271" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-271">&#91;271&#93;</a></sup>  Although Eisenhower never really believed that these allegations were true,<sup id="cite_ref-272" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-272">&#91;272&#93;</a></sup> in January 1954 he ordered that "a blank wall" be placed between Oppenheimer and all defense-related activities.<sup id="cite_ref-273" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-273">&#91;273&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Oppenheimer_security_hearing" title="Oppenheimer security hearing">Oppenheimer security hearing</a> was conducted later that year, resulting in the physicist losing his security clearance.<sup id="cite_ref-274" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-274">&#91;274&#93;</a></sup> The matter was controversial at the time and remained so in later years, with Oppenheimer achieving a certain martyrdom.<sup id="cite_ref-y-s-132_270-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-y-s-132-270">&#91;270&#93;</a></sup> The case would reflect poorly on Eisenhower as well, but the president had never examined it in any detail and had instead relied excessively upon the advice of his subordinates, especially that of AEC chairman <a href="/wiki/Lewis_Strauss" title="Lewis Strauss">Lewis Strauss</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-275" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-275">&#91;275&#93;</a></sup> Eisenhower later suffered a major political defeat when his nomination of Strauss to be Secretary of Commerce was defeated in the Senate in 1959, in part due to Strauss's role in the Oppenheimer matter.<sup id="cite_ref-276" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-276">&#91;276&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In May 1955, McCarthy threatened to issue subpoenas to White House personnel. Eisenhower was furious, and issued an order as follows: "It is essential to efficient and effective administration that employees of the Executive Branch be in a position to be completely candid in advising with each other on official matters&#160;... it is not in the public interest that any of their conversations or communications, or any documents or reproductions, concerning such advice be disclosed." This was an unprecedented step by Eisenhower to protect communication beyond the confines of a cabinet meeting, and soon became a tradition known as <a href="/wiki/Executive_privilege" title="Executive privilege">executive privilege</a>. Eisenhower's denial of McCarthy's access to his staff reduced McCarthy's hearings to rants about trivial matters and contributed to his ultimate downfall.<sup id="cite_ref-277" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-277">&#91;277&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In early 1954, the Old Guard put forward a constitutional amendment, called the <a href="/wiki/Bricker_Amendment" title="Bricker Amendment">Bricker Amendment</a>, which would curtail international agreements by the Chief Executive, such as the <a href="/wiki/Yalta_Agreement" class="mw-redirect" title="Yalta Agreement">Yalta Agreements</a>. Eisenhower opposed the measure.<sup id="cite_ref-278" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-278">&#91;278&#93;</a></sup> The Old Guard agreed with Eisenhower on the development and ownership of nuclear reactors by private enterprises, which the Democrats opposed. The President succeeded in getting legislation creating a system of licensure for nuclear plants by the AEC.<sup id="cite_ref-279" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-279">&#91;279&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Democrats gained a majority in both houses in the 1954 election.<sup id="cite_ref-280" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-280">&#91;280&#93;</a></sup> Eisenhower had to work with the Democratic Majority Leader <a href="/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson" title="Lyndon B. Johnson">Lyndon B. Johnson</a> (later U.S. president) in the Senate and Speaker <a href="/wiki/Sam_Rayburn" title="Sam Rayburn">Sam Rayburn</a> in the House, both from Texas. <a href="/wiki/Joseph_W._Martin_Jr." title="Joseph W. Martin Jr.">Joe Martin</a>, the Republican Speaker from 1947 to 1949 and again from 1953 to 1955, wrote that Eisenhower "never surrounded himself with assistants who could solve political problems with professional skill. There were exceptions, <a href="/wiki/Leonard_W._Hall" title="Leonard W. Hall">Leonard W. Hall</a>, for example, who as chairman of the <a href="/wiki/Republican_National_Committee" title="Republican National Committee">Republican National Committee</a> tried to open the administration's eyes to the political facts of life, with occasional success. However, these exceptions were not enough to right the balance."<sup id="cite_ref-martin_281-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-martin-281">&#91;281&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Speaker Martin concluded that Eisenhower worked too much through subordinates in dealing with Congress, with results, "often the reverse of what he has desired" because Members of Congress, "resent having some young fellow who was picked up by the White House without ever having been elected to office himself coming around and telling them 'The Chief wants this'. The administration never made use of many Republicans of consequence whose services in one form or another would have been available for the asking."<sup id="cite_ref-martin_281-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-martin-281">&#91;281&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Judicial_appointments">Judicial appointments</span></h3>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Supreme_Court">Supreme Court</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower_Supreme_Court_candidates" title="Dwight D. Eisenhower Supreme Court candidates">Dwight D. Eisenhower Supreme Court candidates</a> and <a href="/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower_judicial_appointments" class="mw-redirect" title="Dwight D. Eisenhower judicial appointments">Dwight D. Eisenhower judicial appointments</a></div>
<p>Eisenhower appointed the following <a href="/wiki/List_of_Justices_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" class="mw-redirect" title="List of Justices of the Supreme Court of the United States">Justices</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" title="Supreme Court of the United States">Supreme Court of the United States</a>:
</p>
<ul><li><a href="/wiki/Earl_Warren" title="Earl Warren">Earl Warren</a>, 1953 (<a href="/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_United_States" title="Chief Justice of the United States">Chief Justice</a>)</li>
<li><a href="/wiki/John_Marshall_Harlan_II" title="John Marshall Harlan II">John Marshall Harlan II</a>, 1954</li>
<li><a href="/wiki/William_J._Brennan" class="mw-redirect" title="William J. Brennan">William J. Brennan</a>, 1956</li>
<li><a href="/wiki/Charles_Evans_Whittaker" title="Charles Evans Whittaker">Charles Evans Whittaker</a>, 1957</li>
<li><a href="/wiki/Potter_Stewart" title="Potter Stewart">Potter Stewart</a>, 1958</li></ul>
<p>Whittaker was unsuited for the role and soon retired (in 1962, after Eisenhower's presidency had ended). Stewart and Harlan were conservative Republicans, while Brennan was a Democrat who became a leading voice for liberalism.<sup id="cite_ref-282" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-282">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup> In selecting a Chief Justice, Eisenhower looked for an experienced jurist who could appeal to liberals in the party as well as law-and-order conservatives, noting privately that Warren "represents the kind of political, economic, and social thinking that I believe we need on the Supreme Court&#160;... He has a national name for integrity, uprightness, and courage that, again, I believe we need on the Court".<sup id="cite_ref-283" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-283">&#91;283&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="States_admitted_to_the_Union">States admitted to the Union</span></h3>
<p>Two states were <a href="/wiki/Admitted_to_the_Union" class="mw-redirect" title="Admitted to the Union">admitted to the Union</a> during Eisenhower's presidency.
</p>
<ul><li><a href="/wiki/Alaska" title="Alaska">Alaska</a>&#160;– January 3, 1959 (49th state)</li>
<li>Hawaii&#160;– August 21, 1959 (50th state)</li></ul>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Health_issues">Health issues</span></h3>
<p>Eisenhower began <a href="/wiki/Chain_smoking" title="Chain smoking">chain smoking</a> cigarettes at West Point, often three or four packs a day. He joked that he "gave [himself] an order" to stop <a href="/wiki/Cold_turkey" title="Cold turkey">cold turkey</a> in 1949. However, <a href="/wiki/Evan_Thomas" title="Evan Thomas">Evan Thomas</a> says the true story was more complex. At first, he removed cigarettes and <a href="/wiki/Ashtray" title="Ashtray">ashtrays</a>, but that did not work. He told a friend:
</p>
<dl><dd>I decided to make a game of the whole business and try to achieve a feeling of some superiority&#160;... So I stuffed cigarettes in every pocket, put them around my office on the desk&#160;... [and] made it a practice to offer a cigarette to anyone who came in&#160;... while mentally reminding myself as I sat down, "I do not have to do what that poor fellow is doing."<sup id="cite_ref-284" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-284">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup></dd></dl>
<p>He was the first president to release information about his health and medical records while in office, but people around him deliberately misled the public about his health. On September 24, 1955, while vacationing in <a href="/wiki/Colorado" title="Colorado">Colorado</a>, he had a serious heart attack.<sup id="cite_ref-285" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-285">&#91;285&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Howard_McCrum_Snyder" title="Howard McCrum Snyder">Howard McCrum Snyder</a>, his personal physician, misdiagnosed the symptoms as <a href="/wiki/Indigestion" title="Indigestion">indigestion</a>, and failed to call in help that was urgently needed. Snyder later falsified his own records to cover his blunder and to allow Eisenhower to imply that he was healthy enough to do his job.<sup id="cite_ref-286" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-286">&#91;286&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-287" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-287">&#91;287&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-288" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-288">&#91;288&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The heart attack required six weeks' hospitalization, during which time Nixon, Dulles, and <a href="/wiki/Sherman_Adams" title="Sherman Adams">Sherman Adams</a> assumed administrative duties and provided communication with the president.<sup id="cite_ref-289" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-289">&#91;289&#93;</a></sup> He was treated by <a href="/wiki/Paul_Dudley_White" title="Paul Dudley White">Paul Dudley White</a>, a <a href="/wiki/Cardiology" title="Cardiology">cardiologist</a> with a national reputation, who regularly informed the press of the president's progress. Instead of discounting him as a candidate for a second term as president, his physician recommended a second term as essential to his recovery.<sup id="cite_ref-290" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-290">&#91;290&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As a consequence of his heart attack Eisenhower developed a left ventricular <a href="/wiki/Aneurysm" title="Aneurysm">aneurysm</a>, which caused a mild stroke during a cabinet meeting on November 25, 1957, when Eisenhower suddenly found himself unable to move his right hand, or to speak as the stroke had caused <a href="/wiki/Aphasia" title="Aphasia">aphasia</a>. The president also suffered from <a href="/wiki/Crohn%27s_disease" title="Crohn&#39;s disease">Crohn's disease</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-291" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-291">&#91;291&#93;</a></sup> chronic inflammatory condition of the intestine,<sup id="cite_ref-292" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-292">&#91;292&#93;</a></sup> which necessitated surgery for a bowel obstruction on June 9, 1956.<sup id="cite_ref-293" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-293">&#91;293&#93;</a></sup> To treat the intestinal block, surgeons bypassed about ten inches of his <a href="/wiki/Small_intestine" title="Small intestine">small intestine</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-294" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-294">&#91;294&#93;</a></sup> His scheduled meeting with Indian Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru" title="Jawaharlal Nehru">Jawaharlal Nehru</a> was postponed so he could recover at his farm.<sup id="cite_ref-295" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-295">&#91;295&#93;</a></sup> He was still recovering from this operation during the <a href="/wiki/Suez_Crisis" title="Suez Crisis">Suez Crisis</a>. Eisenhower's health issues forced him to give up smoking and make some changes to his diet, but he still drank alcohol. During a visit to England, he complained of dizziness and had to have his blood pressure checked on August 29, 1959; however, before dinner at prime ministerial manor house <a href="/wiki/Chequers" title="Chequers">Chequers</a> on the next day his doctor, General Howard Snyder, recalled that Eisenhower "drank several <a href="/wiki/Gin_and_tonic" title="Gin and tonic">gin-and-tonics</a>, and one or two gins on the rocks&#160;... three or four wines with the dinner".<sup id="cite_ref-296" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-296">&#91;296&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Eisenhower's health during the last three years of his second term in office was relatively good. Eventually, after leaving the White House, he suffered several additional and ultimately crippling heart attacks.<sup id="cite_ref-drzebra_297-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-drzebra-297">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup> A severe heart attack in August 1965 largely ended his participation in public affairs.<sup id="cite_ref-298" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-298">&#91;298&#93;</a></sup> On December 12, 1966, his <a href="/wiki/Gallbladder" title="Gallbladder">gallbladder</a> was removed, containing 16 <a href="/wiki/Gallstone" title="Gallstone">gallstones</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-drzebra_297-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-drzebra-297">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup> After Eisenhower's death in 1969 (see below), an autopsy revealed an undiagnosed adrenal <a href="/wiki/Pheochromocytoma" title="Pheochromocytoma">pheochromocytoma</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-299" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-299">&#91;299&#93;</a></sup> a <a href="/wiki/Benign" class="mw-redirect" title="Benign">benign</a> adrenalin-secreting tumor that may have made him more vulnerable to <a href="/wiki/Cardiovascular_disease" title="Cardiovascular disease">heart disease</a> during his presidency. Eisenhower suffered seven heart attacks from 1955 until his death.<sup id="cite_ref-drzebra_297-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-drzebra-297">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="End_of_presidency">End of presidency</span></h3>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Twenty-second_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution">22nd Amendment to the U.S. Constitution</a>, which set a <a href="/wiki/Term_limits_in_the_United_States" title="Term limits in the United States">two-term limit</a> on the presidency, was ratified in 1951. Eisenhower was the first president constitutionally prevented from serving a third term.
</p><p>Eisenhower was also the first outgoing president to come under the protection of the <a href="/wiki/Former_Presidents_Act" title="Former Presidents Act">Former Presidents Act</a>; two living former presidents, <a href="/wiki/Herbert_Hoover" title="Herbert Hoover">Herbert Hoover</a> and <a href="/wiki/Harry_S._Truman" title="Harry S. Truman">Harry S. Truman</a>, had left office before the act was passed. Under the act, Eisenhower was entitled to a lifetime pension, state-provided staff and a <a href="/wiki/United_States_Secret_Service" title="United States Secret Service">Secret Service</a> security detail.<sup id="cite_ref-300" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-300">&#91;300&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the <a href="/wiki/1960_United_States_presidential_election" title="1960 United States presidential election">1960 election</a> to choose his successor, Eisenhower endorsed Nixon over Democrat <a href="/wiki/John_F._Kennedy" title="John F. Kennedy">John F. Kennedy</a>. He told friends, "I will do almost anything to avoid turning my chair and country over to Kennedy."<sup id="cite_ref-time_2008_143-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-time_2008-143">&#91;143&#93;</a></sup> He actively campaigned for Nixon in the final days, although he may have done Nixon some harm. When asked by reporters at the end of a televised press conference to list one of Nixon's policy ideas he had adopted, Eisenhower joked, "If you give me a week, I might think of one. I don't remember." Kennedy's campaign used the quote in one of its campaign commercials. Nixon narrowly lost to Kennedy. Eisenhower, who was, at 70, the oldest president in history to date, was succeeded by 43-year-old Kennedy, the youngest elected president.<sup id="cite_ref-time_2008_143-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-time_2008-143">&#91;143&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>It was originally intended for President Eisenhower to have a more active role in the campaign as he wanted to respond to attacks Kennedy made on his administration. However, First Lady Mamie Eisenhower expressed concern to Second Lady <a href="/wiki/Pat_Nixon" title="Pat Nixon">Pat Nixon</a> about the strain campaigning would put on his heart, and wanted the president to withdraw, without letting him know of her intervention. Vice President Nixon himself was informed by White House physician Major General Howard Snyder that he could not approve a heavy campaign schedule for the president, whose health problems had been exacerbated by Kennedy's attacks. Nixon then convinced Eisenhower not to go ahead with the expanded campaign schedule and limit himself to the original schedule. Nixon reflected that if Eisenhower had carried out his expanded campaign schedule, he might have had a decisive impact on the outcome of the election, especially in states that Kennedy won with razor-thin margins. Mamie did not tell Dwight why Nixon changed his mind on Dwight's campaigning until years later.<sup id="cite_ref-301" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-301">&#91;301&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><span><audio id="mwe_player_2" controls="" preload="none" class="mw-file-element" width="220" style="width:220px;" data-durationhint="931" data-mwtitle="Eisenhower_farewell_address.ogg" data-mwprovider="wikimediacommons" resource="/wiki/File:Eisenhower_farewell_address.ogg"><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/90/Eisenhower_farewell_address.ogg" type="audio/ogg; codecs=&quot;vorbis&quot;" data-title="Original Ogg file (112 kbps)" data-shorttitle="Ogg source" data-width="0" data-height="0" /><source src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/90/Eisenhower_farewell_address.ogg/Eisenhower_farewell_address.ogg.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" data-title="MP3" data-shorttitle="MP3" data-transcodekey="mp3" data-width="0" data-height="0" /><track src="https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?action=timedtext&amp;title=File%3AEisenhower_farewell_address.ogg&amp;lang=en&amp;trackformat=vtt&amp;origin=%2A" kind="subtitles" type="text/vtt" srclang="en" label="English ‪(en)‬" data-dir="ltr" /></audio></span><figcaption>Eisenhower's farewell address, January 17, 1961. Length 15:30.</figcaption></figure>
<p>On January 17, 1961, Eisenhower gave his final televised Address to the Nation from the <a href="/wiki/Oval_Office" title="Oval Office">Oval Office</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-DDEFarewell_302-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-DDEFarewell-302">&#91;302&#93;</a></sup> In his <a href="/wiki/Eisenhower%27s_farewell_address" title="Eisenhower&#39;s farewell address">farewell speech</a>, Eisenhower raised the issue of the Cold War and role of the U.S. armed forces. He described the Cold War: "We face a hostile ideology global in scope, atheistic in character, ruthless in purpose and insidious in method&#160;..." and warned about what he saw as unjustified government spending proposals. He continued with a warning that "we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the <a href="/wiki/Military%E2%80%93industrial_complex" title="Military–industrial complex">military–industrial complex</a>."<sup id="cite_ref-DDEFarewell_302-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-DDEFarewell-302">&#91;302&#93;</a></sup> Eisenhower elaborated, "we recognize the imperative need for this development&#160;... the potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist&#160;... Only an alert and knowledgeable citizenry can compel the proper meshing of the huge industrial and military machinery of defense with our peaceful methods and goals, so that security and liberty may prosper together."<sup id="cite_ref-DDEFarewell_302-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-DDEFarewell-302">&#91;302&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Because of legal issues related to holding a military rank while in a civilian office, Eisenhower had resigned his permanent commission as <a href="/wiki/General_of_the_Army_(United_States)" title="General of the Army (United States)">General of the Army</a> before entering the Presidency. Upon completion of his presidential term, his commission was reactivated by Congress and Eisenhower again was commissioned a five-star general in the United States Army.<sup id="cite_ref-303" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-303">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-304" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-304">&#91;304&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="Post-presidency_.281961.E2.80.931969.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Post-presidency_(1961–1969)">Post-presidency (1961–1969)</span></h2>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Dwight_Eisenhower_at_1964_RNC_(cropped1).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Dwight_Eisenhower_at_1964_RNC_%28cropped1%29.jpg/220px-Dwight_Eisenhower_at_1964_RNC_%28cropped1%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="187" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Dwight_Eisenhower_at_1964_RNC_%28cropped1%29.jpg/330px-Dwight_Eisenhower_at_1964_RNC_%28cropped1%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Dwight_Eisenhower_at_1964_RNC_%28cropped1%29.jpg/440px-Dwight_Eisenhower_at_1964_RNC_%28cropped1%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2315" data-file-height="1966" /></a><figcaption>Eisenhower speaks to the press at the <a href="/wiki/1964_Republican_National_Convention" title="1964 Republican National Convention">1964 Republican National Convention</a></figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:LBJ_and_Eisenhower.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/LBJ_and_Eisenhower.jpg/220px-LBJ_and_Eisenhower.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/LBJ_and_Eisenhower.jpg/330px-LBJ_and_Eisenhower.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/LBJ_and_Eisenhower.jpg/440px-LBJ_and_Eisenhower.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2000" data-file-height="1364" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson" title="Lyndon B. Johnson">President Lyndon Johnson</a> with Eisenhower aboard <a href="/wiki/Air_Force_One" title="Air Force One">Air Force One</a> in October 1965</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Nixon_Contact_Sheet_WHPO-0165_(cropped1).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Nixon_Contact_Sheet_WHPO-0165_%28cropped1%29.jpg/220px-Nixon_Contact_Sheet_WHPO-0165_%28cropped1%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="145" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Nixon_Contact_Sheet_WHPO-0165_%28cropped1%29.jpg/330px-Nixon_Contact_Sheet_WHPO-0165_%28cropped1%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Nixon_Contact_Sheet_WHPO-0165_%28cropped1%29.jpg/440px-Nixon_Contact_Sheet_WHPO-0165_%28cropped1%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="859" data-file-height="565" /></a><figcaption>Eisenhower with President <a href="/wiki/Richard_Nixon" title="Richard Nixon">Richard Nixon</a> in February 1969, less than two months before Eisenhower's death</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Funeral_services_for_Dwight_D._Eisenhower,_March_1969.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Funeral_services_for_Dwight_D._Eisenhower%2C_March_1969.jpg/220px-Funeral_services_for_Dwight_D._Eisenhower%2C_March_1969.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="206" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Funeral_services_for_Dwight_D._Eisenhower%2C_March_1969.jpg/330px-Funeral_services_for_Dwight_D._Eisenhower%2C_March_1969.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Funeral_services_for_Dwight_D._Eisenhower%2C_March_1969.jpg/440px-Funeral_services_for_Dwight_D._Eisenhower%2C_March_1969.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1926" data-file-height="1803" /></a><figcaption>Eisenhower's funeral service</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:DDEisenhowerGrave3.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/DDEisenhowerGrave3.jpg/220px-DDEisenhowerGrave3.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/DDEisenhowerGrave3.jpg/330px-DDEisenhowerGrave3.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/DDEisenhowerGrave3.jpg/440px-DDEisenhowerGrave3.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4608" data-file-height="3072" /></a><figcaption>Graves of Dwight D. Eisenhower, Doud Dwight "Icky" Eisenhower and Mamie Eisenhower in Abilene, Kansas</figcaption></figure>
<p>Following the presidency, Eisenhower moved to the place where he and Mamie had spent much of their post-war time, a working farm adjacent to the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Gettysburg" title="Battle of Gettysburg">battlefield at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania</a>, 70 miles (110&#160;km) from his ancestral home in Elizabethville, Dauphin County, Pennsylvania.<sup id="cite_ref-305" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-305">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-306" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-306">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup> They also maintained a retirement home in <a href="/wiki/Palm_Desert,_California" title="Palm Desert, California">Palm Desert, California</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-307" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-307">&#91;307&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After leaving office, Eisenhower did not completely retreat from political life. He flew to San Antonio, where he had been stationed years earlier, to support <a href="/wiki/John_W._Goode" title="John W. Goode">John W. Goode</a>, the unsuccessful Republican candidate against the Democrat <a href="/wiki/Henry_B._Gonzalez" class="mw-redirect" title="Henry B. Gonzalez">Henry B. Gonzalez</a> for <a href="/wiki/Texas%27s_20th_congressional_district" title="Texas&#39;s 20th congressional district">Texas's 20th congressional district</a> seat.<sup id="cite_ref-308" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-308">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup> He addressed the <a href="/wiki/1964_Republican_National_Convention" title="1964 Republican National Convention">1964 Republican National Convention</a>, in San Francisco, and appeared with party nominee <a href="/wiki/Barry_Goldwater" title="Barry Goldwater">Barry Goldwater</a> in a campaign commercial from his Gettysburg retreat.<sup id="cite_ref-309" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-309">&#91;309&#93;</a></sup> That endorsement came somewhat reluctantly, because Goldwater had in the late 1950s criticized Eisenhower's administration as "a dime-store New Deal".<sup id="cite_ref-310" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-310">&#91;310&#93;</a></sup> On January 20, 1969, <a href="/wiki/First_inauguration_of_Richard_Nixon" title="First inauguration of Richard Nixon">the day Nixon was inaugurated as President</a>, Eisenhower issued a statement praising his former vice president and calling it a "day for rejoicing".<sup id="cite_ref-311" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-311">&#91;311&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Death">Death</span></h3>
<p>On the morning of March 28, 1969, Eisenhower died in Washington, D.C., of <a href="/wiki/Congestive_heart_failure" class="mw-redirect" title="Congestive heart failure">congestive heart failure</a> at <a href="/wiki/Walter_Reed_Army_Medical_Center" title="Walter Reed Army Medical Center">Walter Reed Army Medical Center</a>, at age 78. The following day, his body was moved to the <a href="/wiki/Washington_National_Cathedral" title="Washington National Cathedral">Washington National Cathedral</a>'s Bethlehem Chapel, where he lay in repose for 28 hours.<sup id="cite_ref-FinalPost_312-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FinalPost-312">&#91;312&#93;</a></sup> He was then transported to the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Capitol" title="United States Capitol">United States Capitol</a>, where he <a href="/wiki/Lying_in_state#United_States" title="Lying in state">lay in state</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Capitol_Rotunda" class="mw-redirect" title="Capitol Rotunda">Capitol Rotunda</a> on March 30 and 31.<sup id="cite_ref-313" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-313">&#91;313&#93;</a></sup> A <a href="/wiki/State_funeral" title="State funeral">state funeral</a> service was conducted at the Washington National Cathedral on March 31.<sup id="cite_ref-Funeral_314-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Funeral-314">&#91;314&#93;</a></sup> The president and First Lady, Richard and Pat Nixon, attended, as did former president Lyndon Johnson. Also among the 2,000 invited guests were U.N. Secretary General <a href="/wiki/U_Thant" title="U Thant">U Thant</a> and 191 foreign delegates from 78 countries, including 10 foreign <a href="/wiki/Heads_of_state" class="mw-redirect" title="Heads of state">heads of state and government</a>. Guests included President <a href="/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle" title="Charles de Gaulle">Charles de Gaulle</a> of France, who was in the United States for the first time since the <a href="/wiki/State_funeral_of_John_F._Kennedy" title="State funeral of John F. Kennedy">state funeral of John F. Kennedy</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-315" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-315">&#91;315&#93;</a></sup> Chancellor <a href="/wiki/Kurt-Georg_Kiesinger" class="mw-redirect" title="Kurt-Georg Kiesinger">Kurt-Georg Kiesinger</a> of West Germany, <a href="/wiki/Baudouin_of_Belgium" title="Baudouin of Belgium">King Baudouin</a> of Belgium and Shah <a href="/wiki/Mohammad_Reza_Pahlavi" title="Mohammad Reza Pahlavi">Mohammad Reza Pahlavi</a> of Iran.<sup id="cite_ref-Funeral_314-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Funeral-314">&#91;314&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The service included the singing of <a href="/wiki/Jean-Baptiste_Faure" title="Jean-Baptiste Faure">Faure's</a> <i>The Palms</i>, and the playing of the hymn <i><a href="/wiki/Onward,_Christian_Soldiers" title="Onward, Christian Soldiers">Onward, Christian Soldiers</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-316" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-316">&#91;316&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>That evening, Eisenhower's body was placed onto a special <a href="/wiki/Funeral_train" title="Funeral train">funeral train</a> for its journey from the nation's capital through seven states to his hometown of <a href="/wiki/Abilene,_Kansas" title="Abilene, Kansas">Abilene, Kansas</a>. First incorporated into President <a href="/wiki/Funeral_and_burial_of_Abraham_Lincoln" title="Funeral and burial of Abraham Lincoln">Abraham Lincoln's funeral</a> in 1865, a funeral train would not be part of a U.S. state funeral again until <a href="/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_George_H._W._Bush" title="Death and state funeral of George H. W. Bush">2018</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-317" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-317">&#91;317&#93;</a></sup> Eisenhower is buried inside the Place of Meditation, the chapel on the grounds of the <a href="/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower_Presidential_Library,_Museum_and_Boyhood_Home" title="Dwight D. Eisenhower Presidential Library, Museum and Boyhood Home">Eisenhower Presidential Center</a> in Abilene. As requested, he was buried in a <a href="/wiki/G.I._(military)" class="mw-redirect" title="G.I. (military)">Government Issue</a> casket, wearing his <a href="/wiki/Eisenhower_jacket" title="Eisenhower jacket">World War II uniform</a>, decorated with Army Distinguished Service Medal with three oak leaf clusters, Navy Distinguished Service Medal, and the Legion of Merit. Buried alongside Eisenhower are his son Doud, who died at age 3 in 1921, and wife Mamie, who died in 1979.<sup id="cite_ref-FinalPost_312-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FinalPost-312">&#91;312&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>President Richard Nixon eulogized Eisenhower in 1969, saying:
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r996844942"><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>Some men are considered great because they lead great armies or they lead powerful nations. For eight years now, Dwight Eisenhower has neither commanded an army nor led a nation; and yet he remained through his final days the world's most admired and respected man, truly the first citizen of the world.<sup id="cite_ref-318" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-318">&#91;318&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Legacy_and_memory">Legacy and memory</span></h2>
<p>Eisenhower's reputation declined in the immediate years after he left office. During his presidency, he was widely seen by critics as an inactive, uninspiring, golf-playing president. This was in stark contrast to his vigorous young successor, <a href="/wiki/John_F._Kennedy" title="John F. Kennedy">John F. Kennedy</a>, who was 26 years his junior. Despite his unprecedented use of Army troops to enforce a federal desegregation order at <a href="/wiki/Little_Rock_Central_High_School" title="Little Rock Central High School">Central High School</a> in Little Rock, Eisenhower was criticized for his reluctance to support the <a href="/wiki/Civil_rights_movement" title="Civil rights movement">civil rights movement</a> to the degree that activists wanted. Eisenhower also attracted criticism for his handling of the <a href="/wiki/1960_U-2_incident" title="1960 U-2 incident">1960 U-2 incident</a> and the associated international embarrassment,<sup id="cite_ref-&#39;70s_27_319-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-&#39;70s_27-319">&#91;319&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-us_news_320-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-us_news-320">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup> for the Soviet Union's perceived leadership in the <a href="/wiki/Nuclear_arms_race" title="Nuclear arms race">nuclear arms race</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Space_Race" title="Space Race">Space Race</a>, and for his failure to publicly oppose <a href="/wiki/McCarthyism" title="McCarthyism">McCarthyism</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-321" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-321">&#91;321&#93;</a></sup> In particular, Eisenhower was criticized for failing to defend <a href="/wiki/George_C._Marshall" title="George C. Marshall">George C. Marshall</a> from attacks by <a href="/wiki/Joseph_McCarthy" title="Joseph McCarthy">Joseph McCarthy</a>, though he privately deplored McCarthy's tactics and claims.<sup id="cite_ref-322" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-322">&#91;322&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Following the access of Eisenhower's private papers, his reputation changed amongst presidential historians.<sup id="cite_ref-323" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-323">&#91;323&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-millerlegacy_324-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-millerlegacy-324">&#91;324&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-325" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-325">&#91;325&#93;</a></sup> Historian <a href="/wiki/John_Lewis_Gaddis" title="John Lewis Gaddis">John Lewis Gaddis</a> has summarized a more recent turnaround in evaluations by historians:
</p>
<blockquote><p>Historians long ago abandoned the view that Eisenhower's was a failed presidency. He did, after all, end the Korean War without getting into any others. He stabilized, and did not escalate, the Soviet–American rivalry. He strengthened European alliances while withdrawing support from European colonialism. He rescued the Republican Party from isolationism and McCarthyism. He maintained prosperity, balanced the budget, promoted technological innovation, facilitated (if reluctantly) the civil rights movement and warned, in the most memorable farewell address since Washington's, of a "<a href="/wiki/Military%E2%80%93industrial_complex" title="Military–industrial complex">military–industrial complex</a>" that could endanger the nation's liberties. Not until Reagan would another president leave office with so strong a sense of having accomplished what he set out to do.<sup id="cite_ref-326" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-326">&#91;326&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:72-901-1_HR7786_Veterans_Day_June_1_1954.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/72-901-1_HR7786_Veterans_Day_June_1_1954.jpg/220px-72-901-1_HR7786_Veterans_Day_June_1_1954.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="175" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/72-901-1_HR7786_Veterans_Day_June_1_1954.jpg/330px-72-901-1_HR7786_Veterans_Day_June_1_1954.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/72-901-1_HR7786_Veterans_Day_June_1_1954.jpg/440px-72-901-1_HR7786_Veterans_Day_June_1_1954.jpg 2x" data-file-width="504" data-file-height="401" /></a><figcaption>Eisenhower signs the legislation that changes <a href="/wiki/Armistice_Day" title="Armistice Day">Armistice Day</a> to <a href="/wiki/Veterans_Day_(United_States)" class="mw-redirect" title="Veterans Day (United States)">Veterans Day</a>, June 1, 1954</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Meeting_with_President_Eisenhower._President_Kennedy,_President_Eisenhower,_military_aides._Camp_David,_MD._-_NARA_-_194198.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Meeting_with_President_Eisenhower._President_Kennedy%2C_President_Eisenhower%2C_military_aides._Camp_David%2C_MD._-_NARA_-_194198.jpg/220px-Meeting_with_President_Eisenhower._President_Kennedy%2C_President_Eisenhower%2C_military_aides._Camp_David%2C_MD._-_NARA_-_194198.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="174" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Meeting_with_President_Eisenhower._President_Kennedy%2C_President_Eisenhower%2C_military_aides._Camp_David%2C_MD._-_NARA_-_194198.jpg/330px-Meeting_with_President_Eisenhower._President_Kennedy%2C_President_Eisenhower%2C_military_aides._Camp_David%2C_MD._-_NARA_-_194198.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Meeting_with_President_Eisenhower._President_Kennedy%2C_President_Eisenhower%2C_military_aides._Camp_David%2C_MD._-_NARA_-_194198.jpg/440px-Meeting_with_President_Eisenhower._President_Kennedy%2C_President_Eisenhower%2C_military_aides._Camp_David%2C_MD._-_NARA_-_194198.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2966" data-file-height="2342" /></a><figcaption>President <a href="/wiki/John_F._Kennedy" title="John F. Kennedy">John F. Kennedy</a> meets with General Eisenhower at <a href="/wiki/Camp_David" title="Camp David">Camp David</a>, April 22, 1961, three days after the failed <a href="/wiki/Bay_of_Pigs_Invasion" title="Bay of Pigs Invasion">Bay of Pigs Invasion</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Although conservatism in politics was strong during the 1950s, and Eisenhower generally espoused conservative sentiments, his administration concerned itself mostly with foreign affairs (an area in which the career-military president had more knowledge) and pursued a hands-off domestic policy. Eisenhower looked to moderation and cooperation as a means of governance, which he dubbed "The Middle Way".<sup id="cite_ref-jstor.org_327-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-jstor.org-327">&#91;327&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-328" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-328">&#91;328&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Although he sought to slow or contain the <a href="/wiki/New_Deal" title="New Deal">New Deal</a> and other federal programs, he did not attempt to repeal them outright. In doing so, Eisenhower was popular among the liberal wing of the Republican Party.<sup id="cite_ref-jstor.org_327-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-jstor.org-327">&#91;327&#93;</a></sup> Conservative critics of his administration thought that he did not do enough to advance the goals of the right; according to <a href="/wiki/Hans_Morgenthau" title="Hans Morgenthau">Hans Morgenthau</a>, "Eisenhower's victories were but accidents without consequence in the history of the Republican party."<sup id="cite_ref-329" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-329">&#91;329&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Since the 19th century, many if not all presidents were assisted by a central figure or "gatekeeper", sometimes described as the president's private secretary, sometimes with no official title at all.<sup id="cite_ref-medved_330-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-medved-330">&#91;330&#93;</a></sup> Eisenhower formalized this role, introducing the office of <a href="/wiki/White_House_Chief_of_Staff" title="White House Chief of Staff">White House Chief of Staff</a>&#160;– an idea he borrowed from the United States Army. Every president after <a href="/wiki/Lyndon_Johnson" class="mw-redirect" title="Lyndon Johnson">Lyndon Johnson</a> has also appointed staff to this position.
</p><p>As president, Eisenhower also initiated the "<a href="/wiki/Up_or_out" title="Up or out">up or out</a>" policy that still prevails in the U.S. military. Officers who are passed over for promotion twice, are then usually honorably but quickly discharged, in order to make way for younger, and more able officers.
</p><p>On December 20, 1944, Eisenhower was appointed to the rank of <a href="/wiki/General_of_the_Army_(United_States)" title="General of the Army (United States)">General of the Army</a>, placing him in the company of <a href="/wiki/George_Marshall" class="mw-redirect" title="George Marshall">George Marshall</a>, <a href="/wiki/Henry_H._Arnold" title="Henry H. Arnold">Henry "Hap" Arnold</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Douglas_MacArthur" title="Douglas MacArthur">Douglas MacArthur</a>, the only four men to achieve the rank in World War II. Along with <a href="/wiki/Omar_Bradley" title="Omar Bradley">Omar Bradley</a>, they were the only five men to achieve the rank since the August 5, 1888, death of <a href="/wiki/Philip_Sheridan" title="Philip Sheridan">Philip Sheridan</a>, and the only five men to hold the rank of <a href="/wiki/Five-star_rank" title="Five-star rank">five-star general</a>. The rank was created by an <a href="/wiki/Act_of_Congress" title="Act of Congress">Act of Congress</a> on a temporary basis, when <a href="/wiki/Act_of_Congress" title="Act of Congress">Public Law</a> <a href="https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Public_Law_78-482" class="extiw" title="s:Public Law 78-482">78-482</a> was passed on December 14, 1944,<sup id="cite_ref-PL78-482_331-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PL78-482-331">&#91;331&#93;</a></sup> as a temporary rank, subject to reversion to permanent rank six months after the end of the war. The temporary rank was then declared permanent on March 23, 1946, by Public Law 333 of the <a href="/wiki/79th_Congress" class="mw-redirect" title="79th Congress">79th Congress</a>, which also awarded full pay and allowances in the grade to those on the retired list.<sup id="cite_ref-332" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-332">&#91;332&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-333" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-333">&#91;333&#93;</a></sup> It was created to give the most senior American commanders parity of rank with their British counterparts holding the ranks of <a href="/wiki/Field_marshal_(United_Kingdom)" title="Field marshal (United Kingdom)">field marshal</a> and <a href="/wiki/Admiral_of_the_fleet_(Royal_Navy)" class="mw-redirect" title="Admiral of the fleet (Royal Navy)">admiral of the fleet</a>. 
</p>
